content.thinking:
Extrapolating from 4k to 80k using a power law is speculative, and the wide candidate range of 0.11 to 1.03 relies on validation to pick the right one — that's the robustness mechanism. Whether the true optimum at 80k is really lower is unclear, since more data usually needs less regularization, but noisy labels mean a 256-hidden MLP could still partially memorize noise even at that scale.

Given CPU budget constraints (~1.5s per 1000 steps, roughly 26s per run), I can fit about 3 candidates within the time limit, so I need to choose multipliers that span a wide enough range without spacing them so far apart that the picked value ends up off-optimum — the accuracy-vs-weight-decay curve at 4000 samples shows factor-2 deviations cost roughly 0.01-0.04 in accuracy. I'm considering whether training could be sped up further to afford more candidates, but the matmul cost seems fixed, so I'm weighing alternatives like partial-fraction training instead of three full runs.

On the validation side, standard error at 4000 rows is around 0.008, which is discriminative enough to separate candidates with meaningful gaps, and prior seeds confirmed the validation ranking matched the dev ranking. I'm also noting that crowd labels are quite noisy — agreement with gold is only around 52% via an LDA proxy — which caps the achievable accuracy ceiling around 0.63 based on 5-fold gold validation.

Looking at the scaling trend from 1000 to 4000 rows, accuracy climbs roughly 0.05 per doubling with diminishing returns, so extrapolating to 80k rows suggests something in the 0.75-0.80 range if the trend holds, though it's tight against the 0.765 target and weight decay selection will matter a lot. I'm also considering whether ensembling close-performing candidates by validation score could help, since prior seeds showed the "all" ensemble slightly beating top1 when candidates were close in performance.

I'm testing a hedge rule of averaging any candidates within 0.01 validation accuracy of the best, checking it against a 3x-spaced grid at n=3000: across the seeds, most cases only have one candidate within that margin so top1 is used alone, but where two qualify the averaged result comes out close to but not always beating top1.

Overall it's marginally worse, so I'll stick with simple top1 selection and now wait for the background job to finish.
